description: Arksus helps farmers choose the best crop rotation for their land using NASA data (POWER, SMAP, IMERG) plus SoilGrids. A water-balance model compares rotations and gives a clear recommendation with its main reason, blocked options and a note when results are close. Every number shows its source badge. We need teammates in remote sensing/GIS, agronomy, UX/UI or data storytelling.
summary:
Arksus is a free web tool that helps dryland farmers choose the crop rotation that suits their land. In Central Anatolia, Türkiye's main wheat belt, most farmers leave fields fallow every other year out of habit, without seeing whether chickpea or lentil would serve the land better.

For 13 districts, Arksus runs a daily FAO-56 water-balance model over 24 years of NASA POWER weather (2001–2024) with SoilGrids soil data at three soil depths. It compares three rotations: fallow–wheat, chickpea–wheat and lentil–wheat. Each is scored from 0 to 1 on value to the farmer, wheat yield, soil protection (days of bare soil exposed to wind) and soil water at wheat sowing. The farmer sets the weights.

The result reads "Most suitable for this land under your priorities". It always shows the main reason, the options that were ruled out and why, and a note when results are close. Guardrails block any rotation that would cut the following wheat crop below 85% of its yield after fallow.

Transparency is built in. Every number carries a badge: measured, model, official, statistic, literature, assumption or user input. No prices are shown. The model is checked against GPM IMERG precipitation, national station normals, MERRA-2 root-zone soil wetness, MODIS NDVI crop calendars and a Konya field trial, and its limits are stated openly. Arksus turns NASA Earth observation data into practical, honest guidance for sustainable land use.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Arksus recommends a crop rotation for a specific field under the farmer's own priorities. The farmer finds the field on a map, answers five short questions (water, past crops, soil depth, priority, soil test) and gets a recommendation with its reasons. Arksus does not predict profit or give guarantees. It compares options and explains why one fits best.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python engine takes daily weather from NASA POWER (2001–2024) and soil properties from SoilGrids. For 13 districts of Central Anatolia and three soil depths, it computes FAO-56 reference evapotranspiration and a daily soil water balance, then a water-limited yield ratio (FAO-33) for three rotations: fallow–wheat, chickpea–wheat and lentil–wheat. That is 2,808 simulated sequences. The browser scores each rotation from 0 to 1 on value to the farmer, wheat yield, soil protection (days of bare soil exposed to wind) and soil water at wheat sowing, using weights the farmer sets. Guardrails block a rotation if the next wheat crop falls below 85% of its yield after fallow, or if the first-year crop gives less than 30% of its water-unlimited yield in a median year.

VALIDATION

- Water balance closes to 1e-12 mm on every sequence.

- Our evapotranspiration code reproduces FAO-56 Example 18 (3.88 vs 3.9 mm/day).

- NASA POWER rainfall is compared with GPM IMERG and with national station normals, and corrected per district (POWER overestimates by up to 83%).

- Soil water is compared with MERRA-2 root-zone wetness (seasonal cycle correlation 0.87–0.96).

- Wheat after legumes matches a Konya dryland trial: 0.85 and 0.86 in the model, 0.80 and 0.87 in the trial.

- MODIS NDVI is used to check the crop calendar.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Central Anatolia is Türkiye's main wheat belt, and fallow leaves soil bare and open to wind erosion for months. Arksus shows a farmer, for their own land, when a legume can replace fallow without harming the wheat that follows, and when it cannot. The advice is explainable: it names the main reason, the options ruled out and why, and says so when results are close. It is free, bilingual (Turkish and English), works on a phone and needs no account.

TOOLS

Python (engine, pytest), YAML configuration, JSON Schema data contract, TypeScript, React, Vite and Tailwind for the web app, MapLibre and three.js for the maps, Vitest, a separate Vite app for the 3D district map, GitHub Actions for tests on every change, Vercel for hosting and Supabase for optional sign-in.

CREATIVITY

- The engine has no crop-specific code. New crops and regions come only from configuration files.

- Every number on screen carries a badge: measured, model, official, statistic, literature, assumption or user input.

- Every parameter is stored with its unit, source, type and verification status. Unverified values are shown as "assumption".

- A "why this crop" explanation can be read aloud for farmers who prefer listening.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Trust: no invented numbers and no words such as "guaranteed" or "certain".

- Money: prices change every year, so no prices are shown. They are only used internally to rank options.

- Protecting the main crop: guardrails come before any gain.

- Honesty about limits: results are district-scale estimates. The model has no snow, stubble or nitrogen effect, and we say so on the site.

- Privacy: the tool works without an account.

NASA MERRA-2 (root-zone and surface soil wetness, via NASA POWER)
NASA MODIS Terra NDVI MOD13Q1 v061 (crop calendar check)
ORNL DAAC MODIS/VIIRS Subsets API (NDVI point data)
projectRefs: ESA Copernicus Sentinel-2 L2A (via Element 84 Earth Search)
Sentinel-2 cloudless 2023 by EOX (satellite basemap, Copernicus data)
WMO Climate Normals 1991–2020 (Turkish State Meteorological Service stations, via NOAA NCEI)
NSF NCAR GDEX d736000 (public mirror of GPM IMERG)
TKGM Parsel Sorgu (Turkish land registry parcels)
